title: Co-occurring Alterations in Multiple Tumor Suppressor Genes are Associated with Worse Outcomes in Patients with EGFR-mutant Lung Cancer
author: Paul Stockhammer; Michael Grant; Anna Wurtz; Giorgia Foggetti; F Expósito; Jianlei Gu; Hongyu Zhao; Jungmin Choi; Sangyun Chung; Fangyong Li; Zenta Walther; Julia Dietz; Emily Duffield; Scott Gettinger; Katerina Politi; Sarah B Goldberg
text:
Abstract
Introduction
Patients with metastatic EGFR-mutant NSCLC inevitably have disease progression while on TKI therapy. Co-occurring tumor suppressor gene (TSG) alterations have been associated with poor outcomes, however, detailed analyses of their impact on patient outcomes are limited.
Methods
Patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC treated with EGFR-TKIs who had tumor genomic profiling were included. Alterations in TP53 and five additional TSGs (RB1, NF1, ARID1A, BRCA1 and PTEN) were used to stratify the cohort into three subgroups: patients with tumors harboring a TP53 mutation plus a mutation in ≥1 additional TSG (TP53mut/TSGmut), a TP53 mutation without additional TSG mutations (TP53mut/TSGwt), and TP53wt. Patient characteristics and clinical outcomes were assessed in two independent cohorts.
Results
101 patients from the Yale Cancer Center and 182 patients from the AACR Project GENIE database were included. In the Yale cohort, TP53 mutations were identified in 65 (64%) cases (of which 23 were TP53mut/TSGmut and 42 were TP53mut/TSGwt). Although the presence of a TP53 mutation was associated with worse outcomes, the additional TSG alteration in TP53mut tumors identified a subset of patients associated with particularly aggressive disease and inferior clinical outcome in both the Yale and the GENIE cohort. Specifically, in the Yale cohort for patients receiving first-line TKI, those with TP53mut/TSGmut tumors had shorter PFS and OS than TP53mut/TSGwt (PFS: HR 2.03, CI 1.12 – 3.69, P<0.01, OS: HR 1.58, CI 0.82 – 3.04, P=0.12) or TP53wt cases (PFS: HR 2.4, CI 1.28 – 4.47, P<0.001, OS: HR 2.54, CI 1.21 – 5.34, P<0.005). Inferior outcomes in TP53mut/TSGmut tumors were also seen in patients receiving osimertinib as second-line therapy.
Conclusions
Patients with TP53mut/TSGmut tumors represent a patient subgroup characterized by an aggressive disease phenotype and inferior outcomes on EGFR-TKIs. This information is important for understanding the biologic underpinnings of differential outcomes with TKI treatment and has implications for identifying patients for additional therapeutic interventions beyond osimertinib monotherapy.
Keywords: epidermal growth factor receptor, non-small cell lung cancer, tumor suppressor genes, TP53, targeted therapy
Introduction
EGFR activating mutations are among the most common targetable driver mutations in patients with NSCLC 1. These mutations confer sensitivity to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKI) resulting in significant improvement in progression-free (PFS) and overall survival (OS) in patients with metastatic disease 2–4. However, tumors inevitably recur upon TKI treatment 4–6. Emerging evidence suggests that co-occurring genomic alterations in tumor suppressor genes (TSG) may contribute to molecular and clinical heterogeneity 7. Somatic mutations in TP53 are by far the most frequently identified co-occurring alterations with EGFR mutations, with a prevalence ranging from 55 to 65% 7, 8, and several clinical studies have identified TP53 mutations as an adverse predictive indicator in patients undergoing EGFR-TKI treatment 9–12. However, this observed association between TP53 mutation status and clinical outcome is not uniformly observed and several smaller retrospective studies have not confirmed this association 13–15. Therefore, further characterization of EGFR/TP53-co-mutant tumors and their mutations may be informative.
In contrast to TP53, alterations in other TSGs are usually identified in less than 10% of cases 16, 17, and functional and clinical implications of TSGs beyond TP53 in EGFR-mutant NSCLC have not been fully investigated. Previous studies linked alterations in certain TSGs including RB1, PTEN or ARID1A with poor patient outcomes on EGFR-TKIs, however, these studies were limited by the overall low mutation rate in these additional TSGs in EGFR-mutant NSCLC 11, 18, 19. Thus, understanding the effect of alterations in multiple TSGs may help identify patients with limited benefit from current therapies and could shed light on observations to be further investigated at the molecular level.
In this study, we investigated the clinical consequences of TSG alterations in patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC treated with EGFR-TKIs to determine whether additional TSGs alterations impact outcomes in the context of TP53 mutation status.
Materials and methods
Patients
Patients with confirmed stage IV EGFR-mutant NSCLC treated with first-line EGFR TKI at the Yale Cancer Center between 2016 and 2021 were retrospectively reviewed. Patients with comprehensive next-generation sequencing (NGS) performed either on tumor tissue or circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) or with tumor Whole Exome Sequencing (WES) were included in this study (Supplementary Figure S1). Clinical characteristics, PFS and OS were collected for all patients. PFS was defined as time from start of EGFR-TKI to first radiologically identified disease progression or death, censored at date of last follow-up. Primary progression was defined as patients who had disease progression at their first scan after starting treatment. OS was defined as time from start of EGFR-TKI to death, censored at date of last follow-up. Informed consent under the Yale University Institutional Review Board approved protocols was obtained in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Mutational analyses
Tumors or blood samples were obtained either at time of diagnosis (pre-TKI) or resistance (post-TKI) on first-line EGFR-TKI. In a subset of patients (N=34), paired pre- and post-TKI samples (20 WES pairs, 14 NGS pairs) were available. NGS on tumor tissue was performed using the Foundation One® CDx assay (Foundation Medicine, Cambridge, MA, USA) or the Yale Oncomine™ Comprehensive Assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). NGS on ctDNA was performed using the Guardant360 CDx Professional Services Panel (Guardant Health Clinical Laboratory, Redwood City, CA, USA). Genomic analyses were focused on those genes included in all three NGS panels. For WES, DNA was extracted and analyzed as previously described 17. In brief, sequence reads were mapped to the human reference genome (GRCh38) using the Burrows-Wheeler Aligner-MEM (BWA-MEM) program. For all matched tumor-normal pairs, somatic point mutations and indels were called by Sentieon (v.202112) using TNhaplotyper2. For all somatic mutations called, we extracted base coverage information in all samples and considered the mutations that were supported by at least 5 sequence reads covering and present in more than 5% of all sequencing reads. Identified variants were annotated using the ANNOVAR program 20.
AACR Project GENIE database
The AACR Project GENIE registry contains certified genomic data from records of more than 9,000 patients treated at the consortium’s participating institutions 21. Data from the NSCLC cohort v2.1 consortium GENIE 8.1 – public was accessed through the Synapse cBioPortal platform. Among patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC, those who received erlotinib as first-line EGFR TKI with pre- or post-TKI genomic data available were included in this study (Supplementary Figure S2). Patients treated with osimertinib were no included given that most of them had received prior (EGFR-targeted) systemic therapy. Genomic data regarding TSG alterations was available for 182 patients, and tumor mutation rate (number of genetic alterations / genes tested in each NGS panel) was available for 174 patients.
Statistical analyses
Fishers’ exact tests or Chi-squared tests were applied to compare categorical data. Differences between two groups were tested by Mann Whitney U test. PFS and OS were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. To identify survival differences between groups, log-rank (mantel-cox) tests were performed. A multivariate cox regression model including different clinicopathological characteristics was used to define independent prognostic factors with hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals. Analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism 8.0 (GraphPad Inc., San Diego, CA, USA) and SPSS Statistics 29.0 package (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). The NSCLC GENIE cohort mutation annotated file (MAF) data were downloaded from http://synapse.org/genie. For the Yale Cohort, another MAF was created. Both MAFs were taken for visualization and topological contextualization of TP53 mutations creating Lollipop plots by using the maftool R package 22.
Results
Clinical characteristics
A total of 101 patients with stage IV EGFR-mutant NSCLC treated with first-line TKI at our institution who underwent tumor genomic profiling were identified (Supplementary Figure S1). Table 1 illustrates the clinical characteristics of the cohort. Seventy patients (69%) were female, and the mean age at NSCLC diagnosis was 64.1 years. 53% of patients never smoked, 8 patients (8%) were of Asian ethnicity, and the majority of patients (90%) had ECOG performance status of either 0 or 1. Most patients had tumors harboring EGFR exon 19 deletion mutations (57 patients, 56%) or L858R mutations (30 patients, 30%). Compound mutations and other rare mutations were found in tumors of 10 (10%) and 4 (4%) patients, respectively (Supplementary Table S1). Patients received either 1st or 2nd generation TKIs (68 patients, 67%) or the 3rd generation TKI osimertinib (33 patients, 33%) as first-line EGFR-TKI. Twenty-one patients received osimertinib as second-line EGFR-TKI after progression on a 1st or 2nd generation TKI. Tumor genomic sequencing was performed in 37 cases before EGFR-TKI treatment and in 64 cases at primary or acquired resistance on TKI treatment. Baseline demographics did not differ between those with (N=65, 64%) and those without TP53 mutations (Table 1). Interestingly, TP53 mutations were more commonly identified in tumors with EGFR exon 19 deletion mutations than in those with L858R mutations or compound mutations (63% vs 31% vs 3%, P=0.013, Table 1), The presence of a TP53 mutation also associated with baseline liver metastases (34% versus 14%, p=0.03). As an independent cohort, from the AACR Project Genie database, a total of 182 patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC who received erlotinib as first-line EGFR TKI who underwent tumor genomic profiling were included in this study (Supplementary Figure S2). Clinical data for 179 of these patients was available and is listed in Supplementary Table S2. There were no differences in baseline demographics between TP53mut and TP53wt cases in this cohort.

EGFR/TP53 mutant tumors show a distinct mutational landscape
Given that EGFR mutant tumors commonly harbor co-occurring alterations in TSGs, we sought to investigate whether there was a pattern of TSGs that are more frequently co-altered along with TP53. Accordingly, we first interrogated the AACR GENIE database cohort of patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC who received EGFR-TKI treatment. We focused on additional TSGs beyond TP53 that were included in all the genomic panels included in our study: ARID1A, ATM, BRCA1, CDKN2A, NF1, PTEN, RB1, SMAD4 and STK11. Among those TSGs, we found that RB1, ARID1A, BRCA1, NF1 and PTEN were more frequently mutated in TP53mut as compared to TP53wt tumors (Figure 1A). Importantly, alterations in ≥1 of these 5 additional TSGs were significantly more frequently found together in TP53mut than in TP53wt cases (18.1% vs 6.1%, P=0.025, Figure 1A). Similarly, in the Yale cohort, these TSGs (except BRCA1) were more frequently mutated in TP53mut tumors (Figure 1B and Supplementary Table S3), and alterations in ≥1 of the 5 additional TSGs were numerically more common in TP53mut than in TP53wt tumors, however, this difference did not reach statistical significance (35% vs 19%, P=0.19, Figure 1B). Of note, in both cohorts, alterations in ATM were numerically more common in TP53wt tumors.
Given the observed association of the 5 additional TSGs (RB1, ARID1A, BRCA1, NF1 and PTEN), we decided to further investigate them in the context of EGFR/TP53 co-mutant tumors. In addition, previous studies associated these individual TSGs with treatment resistance or worse patient outcomes in EGFR-mutant NSCLC 16, 19, 23–25. We divided both the Yale cohort and the GENIE cohort into cases with TP53mut tumors plus alterations in ≥1 of those 5 additional TSGs (TP53mut/TSGmut), cases with TP53mut tumors without alterations in these 5 additional TSGs (TP53mut/TSGwt) and patients with TP53wt tumors with or without additional TSG alterations (TP53wt) (Supplementary Figures S1 and S2). In the GENIE cohort, TP53mut/TSGmut tumors had a significantly higher median mutation rate as compared to TP53mut/TSGwt (2.1 vs 1.3 mutations/Mb, P=0.003) or TP53wt tumors (2.1 vs 1.3 mutations/Mb, P<0.0001) (Figure 1C).
Next, we investigated whether TSG alterations were acquired during EGFR-TKI treatment or pre-existed in treatment-naïve tumors. In patients treated at our institution with genomic sequencing of paired tumor specimens pre-TKI and post-TKI (N=34), the frequency of TSG alterations (for all 9 TSGs covered by the sequencing assays) did not significantly differ in pre- vs post-TKI tumor samples (Figure 1D). Among the five additional TSGs investigated in detail here, only RB1 was more frequently found in the post-TKI samples (18% vs 9%), however, this difference was not statistically different. Importantly, most cases (79%) were congruently classified into TP53mut/TSGmut, TP53mut/TSGwt or TP53wt in paired pre- and post-TKI tumor specimens with highest concordance rate between pre- and post-TKI cases noted for TP53mut/TSGmut cases (89%) (Figure 1E and Supplementary Table S4).
TP53 mutations mostly occur in the DNA-binding domain in EGFR-mutant NSCLC
To better characterize the TP53 mutations in EGFR-mutant NSCLC, we compared the distribution of TP53 mutations in both investigated cohorts. Among TP53mut tumors included in the Yale cohort, the majority of TP53 mutations (80%) occurred in the DNA-binding domain (DBD) between codons 100 – 300 (Supplementary Figure S3). Among the DBD mutations, these were mostly missense (79.7%), nonsense (10.9%) and frameshift (7.8%) mutations. Multiple TP53 alterations were identified in 11 patients (17%). In the GENIE cohort, similar distributions were found: the majority of TP53 mutations occurred in the DBD (87%) and most of those mutations were missense (74.8%), frameshift (9.7%) and nonsense (5.8%) mutations (Supplementary Figure S3). Multiple TP53 alterations were identified in 2 patients (1.7%). Importantly, among the TP53mut/TSGmut cases in both the Yale and the GENIE cohort there was a similar distribution of TP53 mutations: most TP53 mutations in the TP53mut/TSGmut cases occurred in the DBD (Yale: 84%, GENIE: 91%) and among those missense mutations were the most common (Yale: 85%, GENIE: 75%).
TP53 mutations with concurrent TSG alterations in EGFR-mutant NSCLC are associated with an aggressive disease phenotype
Next, we hypothesized that the TP53mut/TSGmut subgroup may have distinct clinicopathological characteristics. When comparing the relevant clinical characteristics between Yale cohort patients with TP53mut/TSGmut, TP53mut/TSGwt or TP53wt tumors there was no statistically significant difference between the groups (Table 1). However, primary progression on first-line EGFR-TKI was found to be higher in TP53mut/TSGmut tumors compared to TP53mut/TSGwt or TP53wt tumors (21.7% vs 6.4% vs 8.4%, P=0.08, Figure 2A). At disease progression, although the pattern of each involved organ site did not significantly differ between the groups (Figure 2B), patients with TP53mut/TSGmut tumors were significantly more likely to be associated with more wide-spread progression (defined as progression in ≥3 organs) as compared to patients with TP53mut/TSGwt or TP53wt tumors (40.9% vs 15.8% vs 2.9%, P=0.0009, Figure 2C).
We next aimed to determine whether differences in outcomes upon first-line TKI treatment were observed between the groups. Similar to previous reports 9–12, in the Yale cohort, a shorter OS and a trend towards shorter PFS on first-line TKI was observed for patients with TP53mut tumors when compared to those with TP53wt tumors (median PFS 8.6 vs 12.6 months, HR 1.46, CI 0.97 – 2.21, P=0.09; median OS 30.2 vs 48.8 months, HR 1.68, CI 1.05 – 2.70, P=0.035, Supplementary Figure S4A and S4B). Among cases with TP53 mutations, there was no difference in outcome between cases with missense, nonsense and frameshift mutations (PFS: P=0.61, OS: P=0.71, Supplementary Figure S5A and S5B).
Importantly, after dichotomizing TP53mut cases into TP53mut/TSGmut and TP53mut/TSGwt cases, patients with TP53mut/TSGmut tumors had worse outcomes on first-line EGFR-TKIs than patients with TP53mut/TSGwt (median PFS 8.0 vs 10.6 months, HR 2.03, CI 1.12 – 3.69, P=0.006; median OS 30.0 vs 33.3 months, HR 1.58, CI 0.82 – 3.04, P=0.12) or TP53wt tumors (median PFS 8.0 vs 12.6 months, HR 2.4, CI 1.28 – 4.47, P<0.0001; median OS 30.0 vs 48.8 months, HR 2.54, CI 1.21 – 5.34, P=0.0013, P=0.001) (Figures 3A and 3B). We found no significant difference between patients with TP53mut/TSGwt and TP53wt tumors (PFS: P=0.49, OS: P=0.21). Using a multivariate Cox regression analysis, TP53mut/TSGmut status was independently associated with inferior PFS (HR 2.19, CI 1.24 – 3.87, P=0.007) and OS (HR 2.29, CI 1.23 – 4.25, P=0.009) on EGFR TKI therapy after controlling for other clinicopathological parameters (Table 2). Univariate analyses for all parameters for PFS and OS are illustrated in Supplementary Figure S6 and S7, respectively, and further underline the strong predictive power of concurrent TSG alterations in EGFR/TP53-mutant NSCLC.

Among patients who received osimertinib as second-line TKI (N=21), TP53 mutational status was not significantly associated with PFS or OS (TP53mut versus TP53wt: median PFS 3.7 vs 10.0 months, HR 1.50, CI 0.60 – 3.73, P=0.36; median OS 17.5 vs 30.6 months, HR 1.42, CI 0.56 – 3.59, P=0.43, Supplementary Figure S8A and S8B). However, consistent with the results in patients treated with first-line TKIs, PFS was significantly shorter in patients with TP53mut/TSGmut tumors compared to TP53mut/TSGwt (median PFS 1.6 vs 7.7 months, HR 5.93, CI 0.76 – 46.33, P<0.001; median OS 10.2 vs 28.3 months, HR 2.61, CI 0.56 – 12.19, P=0.098) and TP53wt cases (median PFS 1.6 vs 10.0 months, HR 4.27, CI 0.66 – 27.47, P=0.003; median OS 10.2 vs 30.6 months, HR 5.08, CI 0.70 – 36.81, P=0.002) who were treated with second-line TKI (Figure 3C and 3D). Again, there was no significant difference in PFS and OS between patients with TP53mut/TSGwt and TP53wt tumors. Importantly, distribution of T790M mutations was relatively similar between the three groups (TP53mut/TSGmut: 75% of cases, TP53mut/TSGwt: 88% of cases and TP53wt: 78% of cases).
To determine whether the presence of mutations in the five TSGs alone portend worse outcomes in TP53wt tumors, we subdivided the TP53wt subgroup into patients with TP53wt/TSGmut and TP53wt/TSGwt tumors. Although limited by low sample size, in the TP53wt subgroup additional TSG alterations did not associate with worse PFS or OS (Supplementary Figure S9A-D). Taken together, this analysis indicates that additional specific TSG alterations impact PFS and OS in the context of EGFR/TP53-mutant tumors.
To investigate the impact of concomitant TP53/TSG alterations on outcomes in patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC in an independent cohort, we performed similar analyses using the AACR GENIE cohort. For OS and PFS analyses, data for 179 and 155 patients, respectively, were available. As observed in the Yale cohort, TP53 mutation status was associated with OS (TP53mut versus TP53wt: median OS 29.1 versus 54.2 months, HR 1.99, CI 1.36 – 2.91, P=0.001) and to a lesser extent PFS (TP53mut versus TP53wt: median PFS 7.3 versus 9.6 months, HR 1.41, CI 0.99 – 1.98, P=0.059, Supplementary Figure S10A and S10B). However, patients with TP53mut/TSGmut tumors had significantly worse PFS compared to TP53mut/TSGwt (median PFS 2.5 vs 7.7 months, HR 2.33, CI 1.11 – 4.90, P=0.001) or TP53wt cases (median PFS 2.5 vs 9.6 months, HR 2.55, CI 1.19 – 5.49, P=0.0006, P<0.001) (Figure 4A). PFS for patients with TP53mut/TSGwt and TP53wt tumors was not different (P=0.20). For OS, although numerically different, the differences were not uniformly statistically significant between patients with TP53mut/TSGmut tumors versus TP53mut/TSGwt (median OS 25.0 vs 31.6 months, HR 1.30, CI 0.72 – 2.36, P=0.34) or TP53wt tumors (median OS 25.0 vs 54.2 months, HR 2.65, CI 1.22 – 5.75, P=0.001) (Figure 4B). OS for patients with TP53mut/TSGwt and TP53wt tumors was significantly different in this patient cohort (median OS 31.6 vs 54.6 months, HR 1.87, CI 1.24 – 2.81, P=0.005). To investigate whether different EGFR activating mutations affect these observed outcome patterns, we performed subgroup analyses for exon 19 deletion and L858R cases. Given the low sample size after stratification based on EGFR activating mutations, we combined both cohorts for these analyses. In the exon 19 deletion group, differences in PFS and OS between the three groups (TP53mut/TSGmut, TP53mut/TSGwt and TP53wt) persisted: TP53mut/TSGmut tumors had worse outcomes than patients with TP53mut/TSGwt (median PFS 5.0 vs 9.6 months, HR 2.23, CI 1.14 – 4.36, P=0.001; median OS 30.0 vs 36.1 months, HR 1.88, CI 0.95 – 3.73, P=0.02) or TP53wt tumors (median PFS 5.0 vs 10.7 months, HR 2.65, CI 1.30 – 5.40, P=0.0001; median OS 30.0 vs 51.8 months, HR 4.27, CI 1.72 – 10.59, P<0.0001) (Supplementary Figures S11A and S11B). In the L858R group, differences in PFS between the three groups remained: TP53mut/TSGmut tumors had worse PFS but not worse OS than patients with TP53mut/TSGwt (median PFS 2.5 vs 7.4 months, HR 2.32, CI 1.13 – 4.75, P=0.002; median OS 25.0 vs 26.1 months, HR 1.00, CI 0.54 – 1.87, P=0.99) or TP53wt tumors (median PFS 2.5 vs 8.6 months, HR 2.25, CI 1.10 – 4.59, P=0.004; median OS 25.0 vs 44.7 months, HR 1.50, CI 0.73 – 3.06, P=0.23) (Supplementary Figures S11C and S11D). Taken together, our data show that tumors with alterations in additional specific TSGs characterize a patient group that is associated with inferior outcomes on EGFR-TKIs.
Discussion
Although significant advances have been made in improving outcomes for patients with metastatic EGFR-mutant NSCLC 4, 6, patients inevitably develop progressive disease on EGFR-TKIs. Furthermore, there is significant variability in the duration of responses with EGFR-TKIs, highlighting the need to identify subsets of patients with worse outcomes who may benefit from more aggressive therapy. Although co-occurring alterations in TSGs have been described as determinants of molecular and clinical heterogeneity 16, detailed outcome analyses are limited. In this study, we investigated two cohorts of patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC who received EGFR-TKIs and demonstrate that patients with EGFR/TP53-mutated tumors with specific concurrent alterations in TSGs represent a subgroup of patients characterized by an aggressive disease phenotype and inferior outcomes on EGFR-TKIs.
In both cohorts examined, 64% of tumors harbored alterations in TP53, similar to previous studies 7, 8. The majority of TP53 mutations occurred in the DBD between codons 100 – 300, and most of these were missense mutations. Almost all mutations outside the DBD were either nonsense or frameshift mutations. This observed pattern of TP53 alterations is in line with previous studies investigating TP53 mutations in human cancer 26–28. Alterations in the DBD result in a loss of the DNA-binding capacity of TP53 29 and consequently loss of its main tumor suppressive functions 28. In addition, several hotspot mutations in TP53 are gain-of-function alterations that bestow additional oncogenic functions to mutant p53 protein 30. In the GENIE cohort, we identified at least 13 alterations in TP53 that have been associated with a gain-of-function phenotype 31, however, their roles in EGFR-mutant NSCLC remain unknown. We found that TP53mut were associated with a higher overall mutation rate than that observed in TP53wt tumors, which is consistent with prior reports 15, 32. A previous genomic study in EGFR-mutant NSCLC showed that TP53 alterations occur early during tumorigenesis and therefore may allow for increased genomic instability and tolerance for additional genetic aberrations 33.
The role of TP53 mutations in EGFR-mutant NSCLC has been a major focus of prior investigation, yet knowledge about the impact of other TSG alterations on EGFR-driven lung cancer in the context of EGFR-TKI therapy is limited. Accordingly, we analyzed a representative cohort of paired pre- and post-treatment tumor specimens focusing on alterations in TSGs. In our study, we did not observe a significant difference in the overall frequency of alterations in the TSGs we studied between pre- and post-EGFR-TKI paired tumor specimens. Although in our analysis the frequency of alterations in TP53 and RB1 was slightly higher at disease progression, it remains unclear whether these alterations emerged newly during TKI therapy or were not detected by NGS in the diagnostic tumor specimen. A recent phylogenetic analysis of a limited cohort of patients with paired EGFR-mutant NSCLC tumor specimens similarly found that TP53 mutations were not exclusively truncal and present pre-treatment, and that some were sub-clonal and emerged during TKI treatment. In contrast to TP53, alterations in RB1 were uniformly found to be present in treatment-naïve tumor samples 34. In a larger study, alterations in both TP53 and NF1 were more frequently found in tumor samples obtained at disease progression on EGFR-TKIs when compared to pre-TKI samples, however, that study did not include paired specimens 16. Taken together, future analyses of larger cohorts of paired tumors will be necessary to further investigate the phylogenetics of TSG alterations in EGFR-mutant NSCLC in the context of TKI therapy.
We found that alterations in additional TSGs beyond TP53 were more likely to co-occur in EGFR/TP53-mutant tumors compared to EGFR/TP53wt tumors. These additional TSGs included NF1, RB1, PTEN, ARID1A and BRCA1. Alterations in TSGs besides TP53 are usually found in less than 10% of EGFR-mutant NSCLC 16, and therefore, functional and outcome analyses for specific TSGs are mostly limited to TP53. Nevertheless, a number of previous studies characterized the potential role of several TSGs in EGFR-mutant NSCLC. For example, low expression of NF1 was associated with TKI resistance via upregulation of RAS-MAPK signaling, and tumors with low NF1 expression were associated with primary and acquired resistance to TKIs 23. TP53/RB1 co-mutated tumors were found to be enriched for whole-genome doubling and were associated with histologic small cell transformation 19. Loss of PTEN has also been shown to contribute to TKI resistance 24. Although potential functional roles for BRCA1 or ARID1A in EGFR-mutant NSCLC remain to be determined, alterations in BRCA1 were more frequently found at resistance in EGFR T790Mmut than T790Mwt tumors 16, and a recent review suggested that ARID1A loss may promote epithelial-to mesenchymal transition and activate PI3K-AKT signaling in EGFR-mutant NSCLC 25. Importantly, some of these TSGs are known to be involved in cell cycle regulation and/or DNA repair 35–37, and increased frequency of cell cycle pathway alterations in tumor samples is found more commonly at the time of disease progression on EGFR-TKIs 16. Our findings are in line with previous work suggesting that concurrent genetic alterations between TP53 and other TSGs in EGFR-mutant NSCLC are linked to increased cell cycle dysregulation and/or reduced DNA damage repair enabling tumor cells to develop tolerance towards further genetic aberrations 32. Among TP53-mutant tumors, we found that TP53mut/TSGmut tumors were associated with a significantly higher mutation rate in comparison to TP53mut/TSGwt tumors. Whether this difference in mutation burden is due to these additional TSG alterations or whether TSG alterations are rather a consequence of an increased mutation rate needs to be further investigated.
Despite the preclinical evidence suggesting functional roles of these different TSGs in EGFR-mutant NSCLC, studies investigating the impact of TSG alterations on PFS and OS on EGFR-TKI in EGFR-mutant NSCLC mainly focused on TP53 alone given their overall low prevalence 9–12, 38.
Importantly, in our study, we demonstrate that these additional TSG alterations identify a patient subgroup that is associated with an aggressive disease phenotype and inferior outcomes to EGFR-TKIs. These findings were consistent among two separate cohorts of EGFR-mutant NSCLC patients and in cases with exon 19 deletions and L858R mutations. Furthermore, the prognostic role of TP53mut/TSGmut mutation status was independent of other established adverse prognostic factors including brain and liver metastases, and poor performance status. The relative role of TP53 mutations and mutations in the additional TSGs in contributing to inferior outcomes needs to be determined in future larger studies. Co-occurring alterations in TSGs have been associated with poor outcome in NSCLC. Zhang et al. found that East-Asian patients with lung adenocarcinomas harboring ≥2 co-mutations in TP53, STK11 or MGA had a particularly poor prognosis 39. The importance of alterations in additional TSGs was highlighted in another study showing that patients with EGFR-mutant tumors with co-mutant TP53/RB1 had shorter time to treatment discontinuation compared to TP53-mutant cases 19. In line with these findings, a recent study found that patients with tumors with co-occurring alterations in TP53 and in cell cycle modulators like CDK4, CDK6, MDM2, CDKN2A and CDKN2B were associated with poor outcomes on EGFR-TKIs 32. Besides inferior clinical outcomes, we also found that the subgroup of patients with TP53mut/TSGmut tumors was characterized by a more aggressive disease phenotype than TP53wt tumors and TP53mut/TSGwt tumors: TP53mut/TSGmut cases were more refractory to EGFR-TKIs, and at disease progression these tumors were associated with a more disseminated pattern of disease progression. In line with our findings, Zhang et al. demonstrated that, among all lung adenocarcinomas independent of oncogenic drivers, those harboring two co-occurring TSG alterations were more likely to develop multiple metastases at disease recurrence 39.
Our study has several limitations including its retrospective design and relatively low sample size. Due to low sample size and the low frequency of additional TSG alterations, we were unable to isolate the impact of each individual TSG on clinical outcomes. Additionally, although previous studies have found a concordance rate of >90% between tissue-based or ctDNA-based sequencing 40, patients included in our study had either tissue-based or ctDNA-based sequencing data available. Furthermore, our study included patients with sequencing data from different timepoints during treatment given that we found a high concordance rate for the TSGs analyzed between paired pre- and post-TKI tumor samples (79%). Osimertinib is now broadly used as first-line TKI in patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC, however, most patients (66% of the Yale cohort, 100% of the GENIE cohort) included in this study were treated with first- or second-generation EGFR-TKI. All patients included in this study received EGFR-TKI therapy, thus it remains unclear whether the impact of TSG alterations is prognostic or predictive of outcomes. Nevertheless, our analyses in two independent cohorts of patients with EGFR-mutant NSCLC identified a subgroup of patients with EGFR/TP53-mutated tumors with specific co-occurring TSG alterations that was associated with an aggressive disease phenotype and inferior outcomes with EGFR-TKI. These findings may have implications for understanding the biologic underpinnings of differential outcomes to TKIs in patients with EGFR-mutant lung cancer and selecting patients for alternative or more aggressive intervention beyond osimertinib monotherapy.
